intro: “Too” means more than necessary or more than we want; “enough” means the right amount or degree. With these two words you can explain why something is possible or not: “too expensive for me”, “not big enough for us”.
objectifs: Put too (before the adjective) and enough (after the adjective, before the noun) in the right place.
Use too much / too many with uncountable and countable nouns.
Make too … to and (not) … enough to to show a result.
Tell the difference between too (more than OK), very (a lot) and too (also).

sections.titre: Too + adjective / adverb: more than OK
texte: “Too” goes before an adjective or an adverb. It means “more than necessary or more than we want”, so it almost always shows a problem.
Do not confuse it with “very”, which only means “a lot”, with no problem. “This bag is very expensive” (but I can buy it); “This bag is too expensive” (so I won't buy it).
exemples: This coffee is too hot. I can't drink it.
It's very cold, but it's not too cold for a walk.
very cold = a lot; not too cold = still OK.

texte: Before a noun, we don't use “too” alone: we say “too much” with an uncountable noun and “too many” with a plural countable noun (quantities: lessons 58 and 59).
“Too much” can also come after a verb: “You work too much”.

lignes: There's too much traffic in Lagos.
There are too many people on this bus.
too little time, too few chairs

texte: “Enough” changes position: it goes AFTER an adjective or adverb, but BEFORE a noun.
In the negative, “not … enough” means “less than necessary”: it is often the opposite of too. “The room isn't big enough” = “The room is too small”.

sections.titre: Too … to / enough … to: the result
texte: Add “to + base verb” to show the result: “too + adjective + to” and “adjective + enough + to”.
To say who, add “for + noun / pronoun” before to: “too difficult for me to understand”.
Be careful: do not repeat the object at the end. Say “The box is too heavy to carry”, not “too heavy to carry it”.
exemples: The text was too difficult for me to understand.
We don't have enough time to visit Ghent.

texte: At the end of a positive sentence, “too” means “also”: “I like jazz too”. Its position and the context show which meaning it has.
In a negative sentence, use “either” instead: “I don't like jazz either”.
exemples: She speaks Ewe and French too.

formule: too + adjective (+ to + base) · too much / too many + noun · adjective + enough (+ to + base) · enough + noun
prononciation: “too” is /tuː/, the same sound as “two” and strong “to”. It is never weak and is often stressed: It's TOO expensive.
“enough” is /ɪˈnʌf/: the final gh sounds /f/, and the stress is on the second syllable.
In “enough to”, the f and t come together with no vowel between: /ɪˈnʌf tə/.
To show annoyance, people often make “too” longer: “It's toooo hot!”.
erreurs: The film was very good! / The film was really good!
too shows a problem; for a compliment use very / really.
The suitcase is too heavy to carry it.
The suitcase is too heavy to carry.
Do not repeat the object after too … to.

dialogue.contexte: Kevin and Aïssatou are looking for a room for their mother's birthday party in Yaoundé.
lignes: What do you think of this room?
It's nice, but it's too small. We invited eighty people.
Right, it isn't big enough. And the garden one?
That one is big enough, but it's too expensive for us.
Do we have enough money if we share with our cousins?
Maybe. But there are too many steps — Mum's knees are too weak to climb them.
Good point. Let's look for a place on the ground floor.
Yes, and not too far from her house.

mots: Is there enough food for everyone?
It's too late to call him.
more than is good or needed; also (at the end of a sentence)
This box is too heavy for me.
The soup is too spicy for the children.
We can't afford a new car.
to have enough money to buy something
There isn't enough space in the car.
an empty area you can use
He isn't strong enough to lift it.
She was too weak to walk.

items: I can't reach the shelf. I'm not tall ___.
The music is ___ loud. Please turn it down.
Do you have ___ time to help me?
Is the water warm ___ for a bath?

exercices.consigne: Complete with too much or too many.
items: There are ___ cars in the city centre.
You put ___ salt in the soup.
I made ___ mistakes in the test.

exercices.consigne: Add enough in the right place.
items: Are you old enough to drive?

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with the words in brackets. Keep the same meaning.
items: The bag is too small. (big enough)
She isn't old enough to vote. (too young)
The tea is too hot. I can't drink it. (too … to)
The tea is too hot to drink.
The car is too expensive. We can't buy it. (enough money)
We don't have enough money to buy the car.

exercices.consigne: Write one sentence with too or enough for each situation.
items: Your trousers are small around your waist. (tight)
There are ten guests and six chairs. (chairs)
You are very tired and can't go out. (too … to)
I'm too tired to go out.

exercices.consigne: Describe a home, a town or a job that is not right for you, in four or five sentences with too, too much / many and (not) enough.
items: My first flat in Paris was terrible. It was too small for two people and the kitchen wasn't big enough to cook properly. There was too much noise from the street and too many stairs. And the rent was too high, so I didn't have enough money to go out.

a_retenir: too + adjective / adverb = more than OK (a problem); very = a lot (no problem).
too much + uncountable, too many + plural.
too … to / … enough to + base verb (do not repeat the object at the end).
too at the end of a sentence = also; in negative sentences: either.
